title: Resistance and Resistors
notes: **Resistance** measures how difficult it is for a current to pass through a conductor. A good conductor, such as copper, has a low resistance, so charges flow through it easily. The unit of resistance is the **ohm** (Ω), named after the scientist Georg Ohm. In Practical 8.10, a copper wire and a nichrome wire of the same length and thickness were compared: the copper wire had the lower resistance and let a larger current flow, so the bulb was brighter.

A **resistor** is a circuit component with a certain value of resistance. It has no positive or negative terminal, so its **polarity** does not matter and you can connect it either way round. If the voltage stays the same, a higher resistance gives a smaller current, because the current finds it harder to flow. That is why resistors are built into appliances to keep the current at a safe size. Worked example: in Practical 8.9, replacing a resistor with one of higher resistance made the ammeter reading fall.

The resistance of a wire depends on its material, length and thickness. For wires of the same material, a longer wire or a thinner wire has a higher resistance. A **rheostat** is a variable resistor whose resistance can be adjusted. In a sliding rheostat, moving the contact so the current passes through a shorter length of resistive wire lowers the resistance, so the current rises and a bulb gets brighter. Worked example: a short, thick USB cable has a lower resistance, so it charges a phone faster.

callout: Exam tip: when a bulb dims, follow the chain — a longer or thinner resistive wire gives a higher resistance, a smaller current and a dimmer bulb.

questions.prompt: Which statement about resistance is correct?

options.text: A good conductor has a high resistance.
Resistance measures how difficult it is for current to pass through a conductor.
A resistor must be connected the right way round because it has polarity.

questions.why: Resistance measures the opposition of a material to the flow of current.
questions.wrongWhy: Good conductors have a low resistance, not a high one, and a resistor has no polarity. Answer: resistance measures how difficult it is for current to flow.

questions.prompt: Two resistors, of 5 Ω and 20 Ω, are connected in turn to the same cell. What happens to the current?

options.text: The current is larger with the 20 Ω resistor.
The current is the same in both cases.
The current is larger with the 5 Ω resistor.
The current falls to zero with the 20 Ω resistor.

questions.why: At a fixed voltage, a higher resistance gives a smaller current.
questions.wrongWhy: A higher resistance makes it harder for current to flow, so the smaller resistor gives the larger current. Answer: the current is larger with the 5 Ω resistor.

questions.prompt: In a sliding rheostat, the contact is moved so that the current passes through a shorter length of resistive wire. What happens to the bulb in the circuit?

options.text: It becomes brighter because the resistance decreases.
It becomes dimmer because the resistance increases.
It becomes brighter because the resistance increases.

questions.why: A shorter length of resistive wire means lower resistance, so a larger current flows and the bulb is brighter.
questions.wrongWhy: A longer wire raises resistance and dims the bulb; shortening the wire lowers it. Answer: it becomes brighter because the resistance decreases.

questions.prompt: Four wires have the same length. Which one has the highest resistance?
questions.why: Nichrome has a higher resistance than copper, and a thin wire has a higher resistance than a thick one.
questions.wrongWhy: Both the material and the thickness matter, so the worst case combines nichrome with a thin wire. Answer: a thin nichrome wire.
